title: Is the order more than chance?
question: Do gifts and donations fall shortly before the same official’s decisions for the same payee more often than they would if the decision dates were unrelated to them?
finding: Counting only the official who decided or sponsored a decision, a gift or donation from the payee’s side falls in the 90 days before it 21 times; with the decision dates shuffled 2,000 times the average is 21.9 and 57% of the shuffles show as many or more: no more than chance would produce. Counting every supervisor who sat when the Board approved it, the real count is 116 against a shuffled average of 102.3 (16% of the shuffles show as many or more): no more than chance would produce. Both are null results. Lobbying contacts, which should cluster before decisions if the method can see timing at all, number 123 against a shuffled average of 84.7 (within what the shuffles produce).
how: A pair is a payee and an official who received at least one gift or donation from its side. Two readings of “decided” are tested: the official sponsored the Board file or is the single officer named as approving (99 pairs with such a dealing near any of that official’s decision days), and that plus every supervisor sitting when the Board approved it (305 pairs). The gift and donation dates were left where they are. Each pair’s decision dates were replaced by the same number of dates drawn at random from the days on which that same official decided anything for any payee, so the official’s own calendar and years in office are kept; this was done 2,000 times (fixed random seed 20261113) and the count taken each time. “Share of shuffles as high” is how often the shuffled count reached the real one; the gap columns do the same for before-minus-after. A count is called more, or fewer, than chance only outside the middle 95 of 100 shuffles.
limits: The shuffle keeps each official’s calendar but not each payee’s: a payee whose contracts always come up in one season, and whose staff give in the same season, would look timed without any link. A null here does not clear any single pair, and a positive result would not accuse one: it describes the whole set. The strict reading rests on fewer pairs, because a sponsor is printed on only 55% of the Board’s money files. Donors are tied to a payee by the employer they listed, and give on their own account. So are gifts within the limits. The City bars a contractor’s officers and directors from giving to an official who must approve its contract “from the submission of a proposal for a contract until twelve months from the date the contract was approved” (Ethics Commission guidance quoted in this project’s case file on contract-window donations), which by itself would thin out donations just after an approval. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
